reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Headache occurs exclusively during sleep and wakes the patient, often at a remarkably consistent time each night, hence the label alarm-clock headache
It is predominantly a disorder of older adults, usually beginning after middle age
Attacks last from around fifteen minutes to a few hours after waking and recur on many nights per month
Pain is usually bilateral and mild to moderate, without the prominent cranial autonomic features of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
By definition it is not attributable to another disorder, so secondary causes must be excluded
A bedtime dose of caffeine is a simple and often effective preventive, with lithium and indometacin as alternatives
Overnight blood pressure and sleep-related breathing should be assessed, as nocturnal hypertension and sleep apnoea can mimic the syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Hypnic headache is closely tied to sleep and is thought to reflect dysfunction of hypothalamic structures involved in sleep regulation and pain modulation, including the suprachiasmatic nucleus that governs circadian timing. A relationship with REM sleep has been suggested given the timing of attacks, and age-related changes in melatonin secretion and sleep architecture may contribute, but the precise mechanism is not established.
additionalDifferentials: Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
Intracranial lesion causing nocturnal or positional headache
additionalInvestigations: Headache diary capturing the nocturnal timing and duration of attacks
MRI brain to exclude an intracranial cause
Overnight or ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
Polysomnography or a sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected
Review of medications and caffeine intake
redFlags: Focal neurological signs or features of raised intracranial pressure
New nocturnal headache with uncontrolled hypertension
Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas or excessive daytime sleepiness suggesting sleep apnoea
reference.prognosis: The disorder is benign once secondary causes are excluded and often responds well to bedtime caffeine or to preventives such as lithium or indometacin, though it may persist or recur over years.
pitfalls: Assuming nocturnal headache is cluster headache and missing the distinct alarm-clock pattern
Failing to exclude nocturnal hypertension, sleep apnoea or an intracranial lesion
Overlooking the simple effectiveness of bedtime caffeine
Using sedating night-time treatments that worsen sleep-disordered breathing
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Offer a bedtime dose of caffeine as first-line prophylaxis, given its simplicity and frequent efficacy
Use lithium or indometacin as alternative preventives when caffeine is insufficient or not tolerated
Exclude secondary and sinister causes with neuroimaging before settling on the diagnosis, as it is defined by exclusion
Screen for and treat obstructive sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypertension, which can mimic or coexist
Maintain a headache diary to confirm the characteristic nocturnal timing and monitor the response to treatment
Monitor for adverse effects of preventives, particularly lithium toxicity and the gastrointestinal and renal effects of indometacin, in this older population
Refer to a headache specialist or neurology when attacks are refractory or the diagnosis is uncertain
